# Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Abstractions

> Interface-only NuGet package defining `IScheduler`, the contract for handing work to an execution strategy without knowing what it is: 56 overloads in four families - `Schedule` (blocks until the item has run), `ScheduleAsync` (returns a task that completes when it has run), and `UnsafeSchedule`/`UnsafeScheduleAsync` (the same without capturing the caller's execution context) - each taking synchronous or asynchronous, cancellable or non-cancellable actions and functions, with and without a caller-supplied `CancellationToken`. Also defines `ExecutionDeclinedException`, raised when an accepted item is not executed because the scheduler stopped in the meantime. Targets netstandard2.0 and net8.0 and lives in the `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers` namespace.

## At a glance

- **Package:** `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Abstractions`
- **Namespace:** `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers` - the namespace does not carry the `.Abstractions` suffix. `using Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers;` is correct; `using Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Abstractions;` does not compile.
- **Target frameworks:** `netstandard2.0`, `net8.0`
- **Native AOT and trimming:** compatible. The `net8.0` target is built with `IsAotCompatible`, which also marks the assembly trimmable, and is verified by an analyzer-clean build plus a native smoke-test binary published and run in CI. See [AOT.md](https://codeberg.org/DerPeit/Josupeit.Practices/raw/branch/main/AOT.md).
- **Dependencies:** none. The `[PublicAPI]` annotations visible in the source are compile-time only and are not shipped.
- **Contents:** one interface and one exception type. No classes to derive from - those live in `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Core`.
- **Nullability:** every declaration in this document is shown as compiled under `#nullable enable`. An unannotated reference type such as `Task` is non-nullable; nothing in this package is nullable.
- **Authoritative inventory:** [PublicAPI.Shipped.txt](https://codeberg.org/DerPeit/Josupeit.Practices/raw/branch/main/src/Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Abstractions/PublicAPI.Shipped.txt) is the analyzer-enforced list of every public member, kept in sync with the compiled assembly by RS0016/RS0017. Format key: `!` marks a non-nullable and `?` a nullable reference type; members are prefixed with `abstract`, `virtual`, `override`, or `static` where applicable; accessibility is not shown.
- **This document:** ships inside the NuGet package as `llms-full.txt` and is published at https://codeberg.org/DerPeit/Josupeit.Practices/raw/branch/main/src/Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Abstractions/llms-full.txt. The packaged copy matches its package version; the published copy describes the latest release.
- **Implementations:** `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Core` provides base classes that reduce the 56 members to a single override; `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.TaskPool` and `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Channel` are ready-made schedulers (see Related packages).
- **License:** EUPL-1.2

Install:

```
dotnet add package Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Abstractions
```

## Concepts

Different parts of an application have different scheduling needs - fire work onto the thread pool, or push it through a FIFO queue with a fixed number of consumers and pause support. `IScheduler` lets call sites submit work without committing to a strategy, so the strategy can change without touching them.

The interface is deliberately broad. Its 56 members are one idea repeated over three axes:

- **Family** - how the caller waits. `Schedule` blocks the calling thread until the item has completed and returns the function's result directly. `ScheduleAsync` returns a `Task` (or `Task<TResult>`) that completes when the item has completed. The `Unsafe*` twins behave identically but do **not** capture the caller's `ExecutionContext`, so ambient state such as `AsyncLocal<T>` values does not flow into the work item - cheaper, for tight loops where that state is not needed.
- **Delegate shape** - what runs. A synchronous action (`Action`) or function (`Func<TResult>`), an asynchronous action (`Func<Task>`) or function (`Func<Task<TResult>>`), and each of those in a _cancellable_ form that receives a `CancellationToken` (`Action<CancellationToken>`, `Func<CancellationToken, Task>`, and so on).
- **Caller token** - whether the caller passes its own `CancellationToken`. The asynchronous families accept one for every delegate shape. The synchronous families accept one only for cancellable delegates: a blocking call whose delegate cannot observe a token has nothing to cancel.

Two tokens are involved and they are not the same. The token _the delegate receives_ is the scheduler's: it is canceled when the scheduler stops and, in the overloads that take a caller token, also when that caller token is canceled. Do not expect it to be the caller's token instance.

`IScheduler` has no lifecycle members. Whether a scheduler can be started, paused, or stopped, and how, is exposed separately by implementations - typically through `IService`/`IAsyncService`. When a scheduler does stop after accepting an item but before running it, the item's caller receives `ExecutionDeclinedException`.

## Types

| Type                         | Kind      | Members                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------- | --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `IScheduler`                 | interface | 56 methods: 12 `Schedule`, 16 `ScheduleAsync`, 12 `UnsafeSchedule`, 16 `UnsafeScheduleAsync`              |
| `ExecutionDeclinedException` | class     | `InvalidOperationException` subclass with a fixed message; parameterless and inner-exception constructors |

### `IScheduler`

Every member of one family, grouped; the `Unsafe*` families repeat the signatures of their safe twins exactly. None of the members has a default implementation.

```csharp
namespace Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers;

public interface IScheduler
{
    // Schedule: blocks until the item has completed; functions return their result directly.
    void Schedule(Action action);
    void Schedule(Action<CancellationToken> cancellableAction);
    void Schedule(Action<CancellationToken> cancellableAction, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    void Schedule(Func<Task> asyncAction);
    void Schedule(Func<CancellationToken, Task> cancellableAsyncAction);
    void Schedule(Func<CancellationToken, Task> cancellableAsyncAction, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    TResult Schedule<TResult>(Func<TResult> func);
    TResult Schedule<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, TResult> cancellableFunc);
    TResult Schedule<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, TResult> cancellableFunc, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    TResult Schedule<TResult>(Func<Task<TResult>> asyncFunc);
    TResult Schedule<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, Task<TResult>> cancellableAsyncFunc);
    TResult Schedule<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, Task<TResult>> cancellableAsyncFunc, CancellationToken cancellationToken);

    // ScheduleAsync: returns a task that completes when the item has completed.
    Task ScheduleAsync(Action action);
    Task ScheduleAsync(Action action, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task ScheduleAsync(Action<CancellationToken> cancellableAction);
    Task ScheduleAsync(Action<CancellationToken> cancellableAction, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task ScheduleAsync(Func<Task> asyncAction);
    Task ScheduleAsync(Func<Task> asyncAction, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task ScheduleAsync(Func<CancellationToken, Task> cancellableAsyncAction);
    Task ScheduleAsync(Func<CancellationToken, Task> cancellableAsyncAction, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task<TResult> ScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<TResult> func);
    Task<TResult> ScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<TResult> func, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task<TResult> ScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, TResult> cancellableFunc);
    Task<TResult> ScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, TResult> cancellableFunc, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task<TResult> ScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<Task<TResult>> asyncFunc);
    Task<TResult> ScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<Task<TResult>> asyncFunc, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task<TResult> ScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, Task<TResult>> cancellableAsyncFunc);
    Task<TResult> ScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, Task<TResult>> cancellableAsyncFunc, CancellationToken cancellationToken);

    // UnsafeSchedule: as Schedule, without capturing the caller's ExecutionContext.
    void UnsafeSchedule(Action action);
    void UnsafeSchedule(Action<CancellationToken> cancellableAction);
    void UnsafeSchedule(Action<CancellationToken> cancellableAction, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    void UnsafeSchedule(Func<Task> asyncAction);
    void UnsafeSchedule(Func<CancellationToken, Task> cancellableAsyncAction);
    void UnsafeSchedule(Func<CancellationToken, Task> cancellableAsyncAction, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    TResult UnsafeSchedule<TResult>(Func<TResult> func);
    TResult UnsafeSchedule<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, TResult> cancellableFunc);
    TResult UnsafeSchedule<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, TResult> cancellableFunc, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    TResult UnsafeSchedule<TResult>(Func<Task<TResult>> asyncFunc);
    TResult UnsafeSchedule<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, Task<TResult>> cancellableAsyncFunc);
    TResult UnsafeSchedule<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, Task<TResult>> cancellableAsyncFunc, CancellationToken cancellationToken);

    // UnsafeScheduleAsync: as ScheduleAsync, without capturing the caller's ExecutionContext.
    Task UnsafeScheduleAsync(Action action);
    Task UnsafeScheduleAsync(Action action, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task UnsafeScheduleAsync(Action<CancellationToken> cancellableAction);
    Task UnsafeScheduleAsync(Action<CancellationToken> cancellableAction, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task UnsafeScheduleAsync(Func<Task> asyncAction);
    Task UnsafeScheduleAsync(Func<Task> asyncAction, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task UnsafeScheduleAsync(Func<CancellationToken, Task> cancellableAsyncAction);
    Task UnsafeScheduleAsync(Func<CancellationToken, Task> cancellableAsyncAction, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task<TResult> UnsafeScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<TResult> func);
    Task<TResult> UnsafeScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<TResult> func, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task<TResult> UnsafeScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, TResult> cancellableFunc);
    Task<TResult> UnsafeScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, TResult> cancellableFunc, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task<TResult> UnsafeScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<Task<TResult>> asyncFunc);
    Task<TResult> UnsafeScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<Task<TResult>> asyncFunc, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
    Task<TResult> UnsafeScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, Task<TResult>> cancellableAsyncFunc);
    Task<TResult> UnsafeScheduleAsync<TResult>(Func<CancellationToken, Task<TResult>> cancellableAsyncFunc, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
}
```

The same set as a matrix. "token" is a trailing `CancellationToken cancellationToken` parameter supplied by the caller.

| Delegate shape                           | `Schedule` / `UnsafeSchedule`                         | `ScheduleAsync` / `UnsafeScheduleAsync`                     |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Action`                                 | `(action)` -> `void`                                  | `(action)`, `(action, token)` -> `Task`                     |
| `Action<CancellationToken>`              | `(cancellableAction)`, `(..., token)` -> `void`       | `(cancellableAction)`, `(..., token)` -> `Task`             |
| `Func<Task>`                             | `(asyncAction)` -> `void`                             | `(asyncAction)`, `(..., token)` -> `Task`                   |
| `Func<CancellationToken, Task>`          | `(cancellableAsyncAction)`, `(..., token)` -> `void`  | `(cancellableAsyncAction)`, `(..., token)` -> `Task`        |
| `Func<TResult>`                          | `(func)` -> `TResult`                                 | `(func)`, `(..., token)` -> `Task<TResult>`                 |
| `Func<CancellationToken, TResult>`       | `(cancellableFunc)`, `(..., token)` -> `TResult`      | `(cancellableFunc)`, `(..., token)` -> `Task<TResult>`      |
| `Func<Task<TResult>>`                    | `(asyncFunc)` -> `TResult`                            | `(asyncFunc)`, `(..., token)` -> `Task<TResult>`            |
| `Func<CancellationToken, Task<TResult>>` | `(cancellableAsyncFunc)`, `(..., token)` -> `TResult` | `(cancellableAsyncFunc)`, `(..., token)` -> `Task<TResult>` |

Note the four gaps in the synchronous column: `Schedule(Action, CancellationToken)`, `Schedule(Func<Task>, CancellationToken)`, `Schedule<TResult>(Func<TResult>, CancellationToken)`, and `Schedule<TResult>(Func<Task<TResult>>, CancellationToken)` do not exist, nor do their `UnsafeSchedule` twins. A synchronous call with a delegate that cannot observe a token takes no token.

### `ExecutionDeclinedException`

Raised when an item that the scheduler accepted is not executed - typically because the scheduler was stopped between enqueuing and execution. It derives from `InvalidOperationException`, so a handler for that type catches it as well. The message is fixed; there is no constructor that takes a message.

```csharp
namespace Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers;

public class ExecutionDeclinedException : InvalidOperationException
{
    public ExecutionDeclinedException();

    public ExecutionDeclinedException(Exception innerException);
}
```

Message text: `After enqueuing, but prior to execution, the scheduler declined to process the operation. Likely, the scheduler has transitioned to a state that no longer allows further processing. It may have been stopped in the meantime.`

## Contract expectations

What implementers must guarantee and what consumers may rely on:

1. **Completion.** `Schedule` returns only after the item has completed; `ScheduleAsync` returns a task that completes only after the item has completed. For function shapes the result is the delegate's return value - unwrapped from `Task<TResult>` when the delegate is asynchronous. Neither family is fire-and-forget.
2. **The delegate's token.** A cancellable delegate receives the scheduler's token. It is canceled when the scheduler stops and, in the overloads that take a caller token, also when that caller token is canceled. Do not assume it is the caller's token instance; an implementation may hand the caller's token through unchanged when it has nothing of its own to link.
3. **Token-less overloads.** Each token-less overload is by contract equivalent to its token-accepting sibling called with `CancellationToken.None` - a requirement, not a convention, and what the Task-based Asynchronous Pattern prescribes for overloads without a cancellation token. Every token-less member carries this statement in its XML documentation.
4. **`Unsafe*` families.** They do not capture the caller's `ExecutionContext`; ambient state such as `AsyncLocal<T>` values and the current culture set through it does not flow into the item. Under which context the item does run is left to the implementation.
5. **Exceptions from the item.** An exception thrown by the delegate reaches the caller - thrown from `Schedule`, faulting the task from `ScheduleAsync`. Whether it arrives wrapped is left to the implementation. `ExecutionDeclinedException` is reserved for an accepted item that will not run.
6. **Left open.** Ordering between items, degree of concurrency, which thread runs an item, whether submitting to a scheduler that has already stopped fails immediately or is declined later, and whether an item may itself call back into the scheduler - all implementation-defined. Consult the implementation's documentation.
7. **Lifecycle.** `IScheduler` has none. Implementations that stop expose their lifecycle separately, usually through `IService` or `IAsyncService`.

## Usage

### Submitting work through the interface

Depend on `IScheduler` in components that need work executed without deciding how. Pick the family by how you wait, the overload by what you have.

```csharp
using System.Threading;
using System.Threading.Tasks;
using Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers;

public sealed class ThumbnailPipeline
{
    private readonly IScheduler _scheduler;

    public ThumbnailPipeline(IScheduler scheduler) => _scheduler = scheduler;

    // Blocks until the action has run.
    public void WarmUp() => _scheduler.Schedule(() => LoadCodecs());

    // Blocks until the function has run and returns its result.
    public int CountPending() => _scheduler.Schedule(() => PendingCount());

    // Asynchronous, cancellable: the delegate receives the scheduler's token, linked to ours.
    public Task RenderAsync(string path, CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
        _scheduler.ScheduleAsync(ct => RenderCoreAsync(path, ct), cancellationToken);

    // Asynchronous function with a result.
    public Task<byte[]> ReadAsync(string path, CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
        _scheduler.ScheduleAsync(ct => ReadCoreAsync(path, ct), cancellationToken);

    private static void LoadCodecs()
    {
    }

    private static int PendingCount() => 0;

    private static Task RenderCoreAsync(string path, CancellationToken cancellationToken) => Task.CompletedTask;

    private static Task<byte[]> ReadCoreAsync(string path, CancellationToken cancellationToken) => Task.FromResult(new byte[0]);
}
```

Overload resolution follows the lambda: `() => DoAsync()` with a `Task`-returning method binds to the `Func<Task>` overload (and `Schedule` then blocks until that task completes); `() => 42` binds to `Func<TResult>`; `() => FetchAsync()` with a `Task<T>`-returning method binds to `Func<Task<TResult>>`, so `Schedule` returns the unwrapped `T`; `ct => Work(ct)` binds to the cancellable shape.

### Handling a declined item

```csharp
public async Task<bool> TryRenderAsync(string path, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    try
    {
        await _scheduler.ScheduleAsync(ct => RenderCoreAsync(path, ct), cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false);

        return true;
    }
    catch (ExecutionDeclinedException)
    {
        return false;   // accepted, then the scheduler stopped before running it
    }
}
```

### When to use the `Unsafe*` families

Use them for items that neither read nor need ambient state - `AsyncLocal<T>` values, logging scopes carried in `AsyncLocal<T>`, the culture set through the execution context - and where the per-item cost of capturing the context matters, such as tight inner loops. Everything else is identical.

```csharp
for (var i = 0; i < samples.Length; i++)
{
    var sample = samples[i];

    _scheduler.UnsafeSchedule(() => Accumulate(sample));
}
```

### Implementing `IScheduler`

Do not implement the 56 members by hand. `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Core` provides base classes that implement all of them on top of a single `Enqueue`/`EnqueueAsync` override, including the sync/async bridging and the token linking described above. Use `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.TaskPool` or `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Channel` when a ready-made strategy fits.

## Choosing an overload

- Need the result or completion on the current thread: `Schedule`. Can await: `ScheduleAsync`.
- The item must stop when the caller gives up or the scheduler stops: use a cancellable delegate shape and honor the token it receives.
- You hold a `CancellationToken`: pass it - every asynchronous shape and every cancellable synchronous shape has an overload for it.
- Ambient state is irrelevant and the call is on a hot path: the `Unsafe*` twin.
- Tracked, observable background work with results and progress rather than a blocking or awaited call: use `Josupeit.Practices.Jobs` on top of a scheduler instead.

## Common mistakes

- **Wrong namespace.** The types live in `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers`. A `Josupeit.Practices.Schedulers.Abstractions` namespace does not exist.
- **Expecting `Schedule` to return before the work runs.** Both families wait for completion; `Schedule` blocks the caller. There is no fire-and-forget member - discarding the task of `ScheduleAsync` loses its exceptions; use `Josupeit.Practices.Jobs` for tracked background work.
- **Calling `Schedule(action, cancellationToken)` with a non-cancellable delegate.** No such overload for `Action`, `Func<Task>`, `Func<TResult>`, or `Func<Task<TResult>>` in the synchronous families. Use the cancellable delegate shape, or `ScheduleAsync`, which takes a token for every shape.
- **Treating the delegate's token as the caller's token.** It is the scheduler's linked token: it fires on stop and, if you passed one, when your token fires. Compare neither identity nor `CanBeCanceled` against yours.
- **Reading `AsyncLocal<T>` inside an `Unsafe*` item.** The context is not captured; the value is absent or stale.
- **`new ExecutionDeclinedException("...")`.** There is no message constructor; the message is fixed. Only `()` and `(Exception innerException)` exist.
- **Assuming ordering or concurrency from the interface.** It promises neither. FIFO versus parallel, and how many at once, is the implementation's choice.
- **Looking for `Start`/`Stop` on `IScheduler`.** It has no lifecycle. Cast to, or depend on, `IService`/`IAsyncService` for implementations that have one.
- **Blocking on `Schedule` from inside a scheduled item.** On a scheduler with bounded concurrency this can deadlock; whether it is safe is implementation-defined.
